messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 40
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Surgeon
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 49

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises, Olfactory (Smoke): Smoke or fire smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Incomplete Picture: I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Javier Morales was forty, a trauma surgeon in a large American hospital, married for twelve years, and until the wildfire he had thought of himself as someone who functioned best under pressure. The fire began during a family trip in the mountains of California, moving faster than anyone around him had believed possible. What stayed with him most was not a single coherent scene but jagged pieces: the sudden roar as trees ignited somewhere out of sight, the dense air that tasted scorched, the burnt smell that seemed to coat his throat, his wife shouting from the car, and the sight of smoke swallowing the road they had planned to use to leave. He could remember trying to calculate routes and risks the way he would in an operating room, but the memory broke apart there. What remained strongest, when it came back, was an overwhelming grief that hit him before he could organize what he was seeing in his mind, grief for how close he had come to losing his wife and for the helplessness of not being able to control what was happening.

In the months afterward, the hospital became an unexpectedly difficult place to be. Javier worked long shifts surrounded by alarms, dropped metal trays, overhead pages, and the sharp smells that come with cautery and sterilizing procedures. A sudden bang in the OR or the burnt scent from surgical equipment could pull the whole experience back without warning. He described it as the memory arriving fully formed before he had time to prepare, even though when he tried to tell the story straight through he could only grasp fragments and blank spaces. The noise and smell were not just reminders; they seemed to carry the disaster in them, so that ordinary moments at work could become saturated with smoke, panic, and that same crushing grief.

Because the memory came in broken flashes, Javier found himself becoming more wary of the world around him. He scanned for the next loud sound, noticed every trace of smoke, and reacted to faint burnt odors other people did not even register. In the hospital parking structure, if he caught a whiff of exhaust that reminded him of scorched air, his chest tightened before he had fully identified why. At home, a neighbor using a grill or a siren passing in the street could make him feel as if something catastrophic were already underway. The fragments seemed to teach his body that these cues meant immediate danger, and the more abrupt and incomplete the recall felt, the more potent the triggers became.

Javier did not talk much about this with his wife. Instead, when something set him off, he tried to get away from it internally as fast as he could. After a loud crash in the operating room or a burnt smell drifting through a corridor, he would bury himself in charting, scroll his phone between cases, or find some other distraction to avoid sitting with what had just surged up. Some nights after a difficult shift he drank alone in the kitchen after his wife went to bed, telling himself he needed to take the edge off. At other times he retreated into sexual fantasies or initiated sex with an urgency that felt less about closeness than about discharge, as if he could outrun the feeling in his body. These habits made sense to him in the moment because they offered immediate relief from the sudden assault of noise, smell, and memory.

Yet the relief never lasted. The more Javier pushed the memory away with distraction, alcohol, or sexual release, the less settled it seemed to become. He would later be hit by the same sensory fragments with even less warning, and when the memory returned it remained disjointed, missing pieces he felt he should be able to supply. What broke through most consistently was grief—raw, disproportionate to the moment, and humiliating to him when it surfaced in the middle of an ordinary workday. He had begun to dread entering certain operating rooms because of the smell of cautery, and he sometimes lingered outside before cases, composing himself in ways his colleagues had started to notice.

By the time he sought help, Javier was frightened by how little control he felt he had over his own mind. He was still performing well enough that no formal complaint had been made, but he knew he was organizing his days around avoiding certain sensory experiences whenever he could, and when he could not avoid them he was relying on alcohol, distraction, and sex to blunt what followed. What finally brought him in was not only the fear that a loud noise or burnt smell at work would bring the wildfire back in the middle of surgery, but also the fear that the memory would never become whole—that he would remain trapped between missing pieces and waves of grief, forever one sound or scent away from being pulled back into it.
